people.occupation: Major General, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (ret.); later Bilfinger+Berger, FruCon, and the Construction Industry Institute at UT Austin
people.notes:
Chuck was born in Kansas City during the last year before the Great Depression, named for his Uncle Charles and his father's college friend Irving York. His father Paul Sherman McGinnis was a Syfo salesman who taught him discipline, courtesy, and a deep patriotism; family vacations to Bennett Spring in the Missouri Ozarks became a tradition that continues to this day. Chuck was a bright child, skipping grades, earning his way onto the Deep Springs College scholarship in 1944 before leaving to enlist in the Army, and ultimately earning his BS and MS in Civil Engineering from Texas A&M by August 1950.

His thirty-year Army career took him around the world. He commanded engineer units in postwar Germany preparing to demolish rail infrastructure in the event of a Soviet advance; served as comptroller in Korea; built civilian housing in Vietnam after the 1968 Tet Offensive — 1,500 homes in eight weeks for displaced Saigon families; and served as Engineer of the Panama Canal Company during what he and Shirley called their favorite posting. He met Shirley Ann Meyer in May 1955 at the Pentagon, where she was secretary to Lt. Gen. Samuel Sturgis. Chuck had been recruited against Sturgis's four-page list of aide requirements — Shirley had jokingly added 'six feet tall and single' at the end. They were married six months later, on November 5, 1955.

Chuck retired in 1979 as a two-star Major General and Director of Civil Works, one of only six in the Corps. He went on to a second career in construction management, first with Bilfinger+Berger and FruCon, then as a research associate with the Construction Industry Institute at UT Austin. In 1998 he and Shirley settled in Charlottesville, Virginia, later moving to Patriots Colony in Williamsburg. He was named a Distinguished Graduate of Texas A&M in 2002. Shirley preceded him in death in 2016 after more than sixty years of marriage; Chuck continues on, the patriarch of the family.

people.univ: University of Texas at Austin (PhD, Anthropology)
people.occupation: Artist; Anthropologist specializing in pre-Columbian Caribbean iconography
people.notes:
Shirley was born on Easter Sunday 1927 in the tight-knit German farming community of Garnavillo, Iowa, the eldest child and only daughter of Eldo Meyer and Beatrice Backhaus. Her mother died from complications following the birth of Shirley's youngest brother Bruce in December 1933, when Shirley was six. She was raised in large part by her Backhaus grandparents and aunts, and by her father, whose temper was difficult but whose love for her — as the daughter who looked like his lost wife — was unquestioned. She learned to drive at eleven, skipped grade three, read voraciously, and began drawing in the margins of her schoolbooks long before she ever took a formal art class.

After a year at business college in Davenport, Shirley moved to Washington, D.C. in May 1946 at age nineteen to work for the Army Corps of Engineers. She spent nearly a decade there as a career secretary, rising from clerk-typist to the right hand of three Chiefs of Engineers, studying watercolor with Rowland Lyon and Richard Lahey on evenings and weekends, and turning down several marriage proposals because she was having too much fun to settle down. In May 1955 she met Captain Charles I. McGinnis — recruited to be Lt. Gen. Sturgis's new aide against an exacting four-page list of requirements to which Shirley had quietly added 'six feet tall and single.' They married six months later. She traveled the world with him across thirty years of Army postings, painting in Japan, Ethiopia, Hawaii, and Panama, raising three children, and keeping a studio wherever they landed.

Her second act was her scholarly life. She began taking community college classes in Virginia in the late 1970s, earned her BA in Anthropology from UMSL, her MA from Washington University, and finally — at age 70, in 1997 — her PhD from the University of Texas at Austin, with an 1,141-page dissertation on ideographic expression in the pre-Columbian Caribbean. She and Chuck settled in Charlottesville in 1998, and later moved to Patriots Colony in Williamsburg. She died there on February 22, 2016, the day after Jim's 51st birthday, after sixty-plus years of marriage. Her own summary of her life, near the end: 'I have lived a life filled with love and happiness. What more could you ask?' She is buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

Paul was a hardworking Kansas City salesman who worked six days a week at Syfo, a carbonated beverage company, until 1949. He was meticulous about his car, fiercely patriotic (too young for WWI, too old for WWII, he served in the Missouri State Guard and taught himself to play the bugle), and a devoted father who taught Chuck discipline, courtesy, and the love of Bennett Spring, Missouri. He bought his first new car — a 1935 Chevrolet standard for $550 — with money left to him by his Uncle Paul Brown, and drove it through the war. He and Sidney raised three children: Chuck, Jack, and Nancy.

Called 'Sid' by family. Married Paul Sherman McGinnis in Kansas City; mother of Chuck, Jack, and Nancy. Known for being a hygiene perfectionist even on primitive family vacations at Bennett Spring. Visited Chuck and Shirley in Panama in the early 1970s, shortly after knee replacement surgery.
Chuck's younger sister, born when Chuck was eight. A painter, like her sister-in-law Shirley.

Chuck's younger brother, born when Chuck was five. Worked his career at General Motors. Lived fifty miles from Bennett Spring, Missouri, and carried on the family's tradition of visiting the state park regularly.

Patriarch of the McGinnis Clan fan chart (July 2024). Five children with Cora Pauline English. Spent his working life in the tobacco business; an American Tobacco Company shareholder. Maintained a farm in Holiday, Kansas with his wife Cora, where he raised chickens, kept a garden, and drove a 1920s-era Chevrolet into Kansas City on weekends.

Chuck's paternal grandmother. A devout Methodist, a dedicated gardener, white-haired and soft-spoken. She hosted the family's Sunday afternoon gatherings at the Holiday, Kansas farm. She neither smoked nor drank, but indulged her daughters and daughters-in-law by passing around the carton of Lucky Strikes that came each Christmas from her American Tobacco dividend.

Shirley's father. An Iowa farmer of German descent who rented the Meier family farm near Garnavillo before buying his own farm after Beatrice's death. He had a difficult temperament — generous with money, quick to anger — but treated Shirley like a princess because she looked so much like her lost wife. After Beatrice died in 1933, he remarried in 1939 to Dolores Sabaan, the local high school teacher, and raised three more children. He died in November 1961.

Shirley's mother. Daughter of Emma Meier and August Backhaus of Garnavillo, Iowa. Popular in the community and deeply loved by her family. She died on December 2, 1933, two weeks after the birth of her youngest son Bruce, from complications following a gallbladder operation — Shirley was six years old. Her loss shaped the rest of Shirley's childhood, and her absence was felt across the whole Backhaus-Meyer community.
